item.title: Al-Arafah Islami Bank holds leadership development training
item.description:
A daylong training program titled “Connect, Influence & Grow: Leadership Development & Interpersonal Excellence” was held at Al-Arafah Islami Bank Training Institute (AIBTI), aiming to enhance the leadership qualities, interpersonal skills and professional excellence of the Bank’s Senior Executives and Managers.
The program was inaugurated on November 10, Tuesday, by the bank’s managing director Mohd Rafat Ullah Khan, who attended as chief guest.
The session was chaired by principal of AIBTI Md Abdur Rahim Duary.
Mohd Rafat Ullah Khan emphasized that effective leadership, efficient communication, mutual collaboration and accountability are essential for achieving institutional goals in an evolving banking environment.
Alongside professional knowledge, he highlighted the importance of developing leadership qualities, team coordination and the ability to make positive decisions.
He expressed his optimism that such training programs would play a significant role in enhancing both the individual and institutional performance of the Bank’s officials.
The training program was facilitated by Khandaker Zia Hasan, founder and chief executive officer of Zia’s Language Centre, Canada, who attended as resource person.
Through practical discussions and experience-sharing sessions, he presented various strategies for developing leadership skills.
A total of 40 Senior Executives and Managers of the Bank participated in the training program.
The day-long session covered various aspects of leadership concepts and development, emotional intelligence, communication skills, interpersonal relationship building, fostering mutual trust and enhancing team effectiveness.
These competencies are expected to contribute to improved workplace performance and enhanced customer service.

item.title: Community Bank extends Tk1.3cr CSR support to Bangladesh Police Institutions
item.description:
Community Bank Bangladesh PLC has provided Tk1.30 crore from its CSR fund to three Bangladesh Police institutions to support healthcare, education and childcare.
The bank allocated Tk1 crore to APBN Medical Center in Uttara, Dhaka, to strengthen its healthcare services and Tk20 lakh to APBN School in Uttara to support its educational programs.
APBN Day-Care Center received Tk10 lakh to improve its facilities.
Md Ali Hossain Fakir, Inspector General of Police and chairman of Community Bank Bangladesh PLC, handed over the cheques alongside Mohammed Emtiaz Uddin, the bank’s managing director.
The heads of the three institutions received the cheques in the presence of senior officials from Bangladesh Police and the bank.
Under the leadership of its managing director, Community Bank continues to advance its commitment to social development and public welfare by strengthening institutions that expand opportunities for children and provide essential services to families.

item.title: Trends Bird, East West Chemicals sign strategic MoU
item.description:
Trends Bird Limited (TBL) and East West Chemicals Limited (EWCL) have recently signed a significant Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), marking the beginning of a strategic collaboration aimed at developing and implementing a customized Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system for EWCL.
Under the collaboration, Trends Bird Limited will design, develop, implement, deploy and hand over a customized Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system for East West Chemicals Limited.
The system is intended to bring EWCL's major operational, commercial, financial and management processes together on one platform, replacing separate working methods with a connected, data-driven approach.
The ERP will cover key areas of EWCL's business, including procurement and inventory, import and LC management, quality control, batch and expiry management, depot and distribution management, sales, delivery and collection, finance and accounts, audit and management controls, and HR and field force functions.
The collaboration reflects a shared vision of strengthening EWCL's digital capability and building a lasting working relationship between the two companies.

item.title: Act early, Live life Shukhee
item.description:
Millions of people in Bangladesh live with diabetes without knowing it, and many discover it only when complications have already reached their eyes, kidneys, heart or feet. Yet with early screening, timely care and simple changes in daily life, diabetes can be prevented, delayed and managed well. To mark World Diabetes Day under the global theme "Early action on diabetes", Grameen HealthTech Limited (Shukhee), in partnership with Experto ReWell, hosted a seminar titled "Act Early, Live Life Shukhee" on 10 November 2026 at Telecom Bhaban.
Mohammad Solaimun Rasel, CTO and CBO of GHL, inaugurated the session. Md. Ashraful Hassan, Chairman, Grameen Group, attended as Chief Guest. He said, "Grameen's journey began with a belief in standing beside people. Today, that same belief is carrying us to the doorstep of healthcare. Through our eye hospitals, a person regains their sight; through safe sanitation, a family gets the foundation of a healthy life; and through digital initiatives like Shukhee, even people in remote villages receive quality medical care. We believe that only healthy people can build a prosperous society. Our commitment is to bring healthcare to every person through the power of social business." Dr. Ahmed Armaan Siddiqui, Chief Executive Officer of GHL/Shukhee, shared his vision of one ecosystem with a shared preventive health mission, from screening to measurable health outcomes. Mohammad Moinul Hakim, CEO of Experto ReWell, presented EverGreen Health™, LinX CGM and Whole-Body Digital Twin technology, showing how screening can lead to precision prevention.
An expert session was conducted by Prof. Dr. Md. Robed Amin, Professor of Medicine, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Prof. Dr. Md. Feroz Amin, Director, BIRDEM, Dr. Hurjahan Banu (Urmi), Associate Professor of Endocrinology and Metabolism, Bangladesh Medical University. Also present were Brig Gen Dr. Md. Jalal Uddin (Retd), Advisor to the Chairman, Grameen Telecom Trust and other high officials.

item.title: E-CAB election tensions escalate amid obstruction and assault allegations
item.description:
Tensions have escalated ahead of the December 19 E-Commerce Association of Bangladesh (E-CAB) election, with candidates alleging physical assaults, intimidation and attempts to prevent them from collecting nomination papers.
In the latest incident on Wednesday, Hosne Ara Nuri, also known as Nowrin, a candidate for the post of general secretary, was taken to Dhanmondi West Police Station by a group of people after she went to the association's office in Dhanmondi to collect her nomination paper.
Videos of the incident have circulated on social media, showing a group of people surrounding her and taking her to the police station.
Nowrin had obtained police clearance on November 9 and deposited Tk1 lakh with E-CAB on November 10 as part of the election process.
Hours before the incident, Nowrin had told the media that she felt unsafe while attempting to participate in the election.
She alleged that followers of Kazi Mukituzzaman Mukit, who is reportedly associated with Jubo Dal, and a few others had been gathering near the E-CAB office throughout the day, creating an intimidating environment.
"Ordinary E-CAB members want the organization’s leadership to be elected through voting in a festive atmosphere. However, followers of Kazi Mukituzzaman Mukit and a few others, including people associated with Jubo Dal, have been sitting near the E-CAB office with groups of people throughout the day, creating disorder. On Tuesday, Mukit's followers tore up the nomination paper of a presidential candidate. Now I am also afraid to collect my nomination paper," she said.
A few hours later, when she went to collect her nomination paper, a group of people allegedly labelled her a collaborator of the previous authoritarian regime and took her to the police station.
Several E-CAB members have alleged that Mukit was behind the incident. However, the allegation could not be independently verified.
An E-CAB member, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Nowrin was a popular candidate and that the incident appeared to be an attempt to prevent her from contesting by delaying the collection of her nomination paper until the deadline passed.
The latest incident came a day after another candidate's representative alleged that he was assaulted and his nomination paper torn up at the E-CAB office on Tuesday, November 10.
However, nomination papers can be collected until November 12, 2026.
According to a written complaint sent by email to Dhanmondi police, the complainant, Mohammad Kawsar Jahan, head of HR and administration at Labaid Cancer Hospital, said he had collected a nomination paper on behalf of Labaid Group Managing Director Sakif Shamiim, who intends to contest the post of president.
He alleged that shortly after leaving the office at around 3:30pm, a group of people attacked and physically assaulted him before tearing up the nomination paper.
He described the incident as an attempt by an interested group to obstruct the upcoming 2026-28 election and undermine a democratic and competitive electoral process.
An E-CAB member alleged that the incident was linked to efforts to prevent Shamiim from contesting. He also claimed that Jannatul Shapla, wife of Narsingdi-5 MP Engineer Ashraf Uddin Bakul, intends to contest the presidential post.
The member further alleged that some individuals had informally formed a panel and were attempting to secure positions without facing competition. E-CAB has no officially announced panel for this year's election.
Contacted over Wednesday's incident, Dhanmondi police station Officer-in-Charge Imdadul Islam Tayeb said Nowrin had been kept at the station for her own safety.
"We have checked everything and found nothing against her. Considering the situation, we will release her shortly," he said.
Asked what measures E-CAB would take to ensure candidates' safety and an inclusive election, Election Committee Chairman Mustafiz said the committee was not responsible for such matters.
"Our responsibility is limited to preparing the voter list and organising the election. Who contests and who does not is not my concern. The E-CAB administrator will look into these matters," he said.
However, when contacted, E-CAB Administrator Sharif Mustafiz said the matter fell under the responsibility of the election commission chairman.
Neither the election committee chairman nor the administrator provided a clear account of what measures would be taken to prevent further incidents and ensure a safe environment for candidates.

item.title: JnU announces admission test schedule for 2026-27 academic year
item.description:
Jagannath University (JnU) has announced the admission test schedule for first-year undergraduate (honours) and BBA programmes for the 2026-27 academic year.
Applications will open on November 25, while admission tests for five units will be held from January 1 to January 23.
The information was announced in an admission circular signed by JnU Acting Registrar Prof Dr Sheikh Md Gias Uddin on Wednesday.
According to the circular, applicants can submit their applications online from 12pm on November 25 until 11:59pm on December 10 through the university's admission website: https://admission.jnu.ac.bd .
The application fee has been set at Tk1,200 for Units A, B, C and D, and Tk1,500 for Unit E.
The admission test schedule is as follows:
All admission tests will be held from 10am to 11am.
According to the circular, students who passed their SSC or equivalent examinations in 2023 or 2024 and their HSC or equivalent examinations in 2026 will be eligible to apply, subject to meeting the prescribed requirements.
Students who failed in up to two subjects in their HSC or equivalent examinations may also apply, provided they meet the SSC or equivalent eligibility requirements.
However, applications will be cancelled if candidates fail to meet the admission eligibility criteria for their respective units after passing the HSC or equivalent examinations.
Foreign students will also be eligible to apply, subject to fulfilling the prescribed requirements.

item.title: Students caught between digital learning and screen addiction
item.description:
Smartphones are increasingly accessible to students, from secondary school to even primary school, offering access to online classes, information and educational content. However, growing use of social media, online games and entertainment has raised concerns about addiction, declining concentration, sleep disruption and risks to physical and mental health.
The debate now centres on how to balance the educational benefits of technology with the need to protect children through age-based guidelines, parental supervision and institutional oversight.
According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) ICT Usage and Application Survey for the April-June quarter of FY2025-26, 89.6% of people aged five and above use mobile phones, up from 88.2% in the same period a year earlier. Smartphone use stood at 75.1%, while 65.6% of people owned a mobile phone. Nearly 99% of households had access to mobile phones.
Internet use among people aged five and above stood at 59.2%, compared with 55% a year earlier. However, only 58.2% of households had internet connections, highlighting the digital divide between access to devices and connectivity.
There are no recent nationwide figures on personal mobile phone use among primary and secondary school students. A 2021 study published in an international journal's Health Science Reports , based on 1,803 secondary school students across 21 districts, found that 67.11% used mobile phones daily. The study, which drew on 2020 data, also linked device use to headaches, back pain, vision problems and sleep disturbances.
Smartphones can help students access online lessons, educational videos, information and language-learning resources, particularly in remote areas. However, excessive use can eat into study time, disrupt sleep and discourage physical activity and outdoor play.
Psychiatrist Dr Mekhla Sarkar said smartphones are designed to encourage prolonged use, making children and adolescents particularly vulnerable to addiction.
Warning signs include steadily increasing screen time, declining academic performance, reduced interest in sports, strained family and peer relationships, and irregular sleeping and eating habits, she said.
Sarkar warned that excessive smartphone use could affect children's physical development, increase the risk of obesity and eye problems, and undermine their social skills. Spending too much time in virtual environments could also make it harder for children to develop realistic expectations and cope with challenges in everyday life.
The Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE) issued a directive in October 2017 restricting the use of mobile phones by students and teachers in classrooms. However, questions remain over its implementation.
DSHE Director General Prof Dr Khan Moinuddin Al Mahmud Sohel said a complete ban on mobile phones was not practical, but students should not have unrestricted access to them. He said discussions had taken place on formulating guidelines to prevent addiction and help students focus on their studies.
Education Minister Dr ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon and State Minister for Primary and Mass Education Bobby Hajjaj have also called for responsible parental supervision and coordinated efforts involving families, schools and communities.
Educationist Rasheda K Chowdhury said restrictions must extend beyond schools to homes, with parents playing an active role. She called for blocking harmful content and providing children with opportunities to participate in sports, storytelling, art and other creative activities.
Cybersecurity expert Arif Moinuddin recommended strict controls on smartphone use during class hours, along with screen-time limits and more extracurricular activities, including debates, sports, science clubs and technology fairs.
Education researcher KM Enamul Haque said a blanket ban would overlook the growing role of digital devices in education. Instead, he suggested introducing age- and institution-specific rules that clearly define when, where and why students may use smartphones and other devices.
Education stakeholders say a coordinated approach combining age-based national guidelines, parental supervision, school-level rules and alternative activities is needed to ensure that children use technology safely and for educational purposes.

item.title: Mir Mugdho memorial defaced again in Brahmanbaria
item.description:
A memorial dedicated to July uprising martyr Mir Mugdho in Chinair of Brahmanbaria Sadar upazila has been defaced with black paint again, obscuring much of his portrait and name.
Local resident and Jubo Dal leader Md Uzzal Ahmed confirmed the incident. He said he noticed the defacement on Wednesday afternoon, adding that the memorial had been similarly defaced before.
Ripan Das, inspector (investigation) of Brahmanbaria Sadar Police Station, said police visited the site after receiving reports of the incident.
He said police were investigating how the memorial was defaced and who was responsible.
On November 25, 2025, the memorial in Chinair was similarly defaced with black paint. However, those responsible for that incident were never identified.

item.title: Four-star Bangladesh down Sri Lanka to finish as group winners
item.description:
Hamza Choudhury, Shamit Shome, Farhaan Ali Wahid and Rakib Hossain scored a goal each as Bangladesh produced a commanding 4-0 victory over Sri Lanka in their second and final Group A fixture at the National Stadium, Dhaka on Wednesday.
With two wins from as many matches, the men in red and green, who had already secured a semi-final berth before the match, finished the group stage as leaders.
Bangladesh head coach Thomas Dooley made three changes to the starting XI, handing Hamza and Farhaan their first starts of the tournament after the two late arrivals joined the national team ahead of the Sri Lanka fixture.
Faisal Fahim and Jamal Bhuiyan were left out, while the third change saw Mohammad Ibrahim replace Bishwanath Ghosh, who picked up an injury during training the day after Bangladesh's 1-0 victory over Bhutan.
Bangladesh put Sri Lanka under pressure from the outset, with Hamza's free-kick in the sixth minute sailing over the crossbar after Rakib earned a set-piece opportunity just outside the box.
Shamit broke the deadlock two minutes later with a volley from the edge of the box after Sri Lankan goalkeeper Sujan Perera punched away Hamza's cross. Shamit's initial volley was blocked by the defence, but the midfielder made no mistake with his second attempt.
Hamza showcased his impressive technique in the 25th minute with a spectacular backheel effort that narrowly missed the target. A quick move down the left flank ended with Shamit heading a long ball into Hamza's path. The Leicester City midfielder beat the advancing goalkeeper to the ball but, with little time to react, attempted a backheel that went just wide.
Shamit tested Perera again in the 42nd minute with a low effort from around 20 yards, but the goalkeeper produced a diving save.
Hamza started as the attacking midfielder behind Ibrahim but frequently switched positions with the striker, who also drifted to the left, allowing Hamza to operate as the central striker at times.
The Leicester City midfielder doubled Bangladesh's lead in the 44th minute. Receiving a through ball from Ibrahim, Hamza surged into the box before beating the goalkeeper with a fiery finish.
Farhaan produced arguably the most eye-catching moment of the match to score Bangladesh's third goal seven minutes into the second half.
The UK-based winger drove into the box from the left, danced past two defenders, beat another with his dribbling skills and capped the brilliant solo run with a clinical finish.
Rakib put the result beyond doubt in the 87th minute with another fine finish to complete Bangladesh's four-goal rout.
Bangladesh will face Pakistan in the second semi-final on Saturday, following the first last-four clash between India and Bhutan at the same venue.

item.title: A friend in Türkiye
item.description:
The meeting between Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in Antalya presents a promising opportunity to strengthen Bangladesh's relationship with Türkiye, with the discussions covering urgent subjects like trade, investment, defense, energy, climate change, and the Rohingya crisis.
Türkiye has emerged as an important partner for Bangladesh, and there is considerable scope to expand that relationship. Greater bilateral trade, Turkish investment in Bangladesh, and cooperation in sectors such as renewable energy, mineral resources, and aviation could open new avenues for economic growth.
The proposed expansion of defence cooperation, including opportunities for joint investment, also deserves careful consideration -- provided it serves our long-term national interests.
Climate change, however, must remain central to Bangladesh's international engagement. As one of the countries most vulnerable to its effects despite contributing very little to global emissions, Bangladesh needs stronger international support.
To that end, the prime minister's participation in COP31 offers an important platform to demand climate finance, greater assistance for adaptation, and meaningful commitments on loss and damage. Türkiye's interest in supporting flood management and climate-resilient infrastructure could also provide opportunities for practical cooperation.
The Rohingya crisis was another important issue raised during the meeting. Türkiye's continued humanitarian assistance and diplomatic support are valuable, and Bangladesh must continue seeking its cooperation in securing safe, dignified, and sustainable repatriation.
There is also potential to strengthen cooperation through jute promotion, particularly as Bangladesh seeks environmentally friendly alternatives to plastic and new international markets for its jute products.
These discussions indicate that Bangladesh-Türkiye relations can move beyond traditional diplomatic engagement towards a more strategic partnership.
However, goodwill and promising conversations alone will not deliver results. The priority now must be to translate these discussions into tangible outcomes.
Both governments must follow through with concrete agreements, investment, and sustained cooperation. Bangladesh should seize this opportunity to build a relationship that delivers lasting economic and diplomatic benefits.

item.title: Making progress with financial inclusion
item.description:
It is encouraging to learn that, according to the National Financial Inclusion Survey 2025, 64.5% of the country's adult population now has access to formal financial services -- a clear sign of Bangladesh making progress in financial inclusion.
This is undoubtedly a positive step towards building a more financially secure and inclusive economy. The expansion of mobile financial services, agent banking, and digital payment facilities has played an important role in bringing more people into the formal financial system.
These services have made financial transactions more accessible, particularly for people in rural areas who may not have easy access to traditional banking facilities, and their continued growth demonstrates how technology, when used effectively, can help bridge longstanding gaps in financial access.
However, the fact that 35.5% of adults remain outside the formal financial system should not be overlooked.
Financial inclusion must extend beyond simply opening accounts. Women, low-income households, informal workers, and people with limited education continue to face barriers that prevent them from accessing and benefiting from financial services. The gender gap is particularly concerning, with women's financial inclusion rate trailing that of men.
Addressing these disparities requires sustained efforts from Bangladesh Bank, financial institutions, and policy-makers.
Banks and other service providers must make their products more affordable, accessible, and convenient -- particularly for those with limited financial resources. Financial literacy programs also need to be strengthened so that people understand how to use these services safely and effectively.
Account holders must also be enabled to actively use their accounts rather than allowing them to remain dormant. Better consumer protection, transparent charges, and reliable digital infrastructure will be essential in building public confidence.
The progress made so far deserves recognition, but it should serve as motivation to do more. Financial inclusion is fundamental to economic participation and opportunity, and we must continue working towards a system where no one is compelled to be left behind.

item.title: Climate resilience must be accessible by design
item.description:
With COP31 ongoing in Antalya, Türkiye, conversation centres on climate finance, adaptation, and loss and damage. One question must accompany these priorities: Who can actually access the protection that climate investments are intended to provide?
A cyclone warning may reach a village without reaching everyone in it. A storm-resistant shelter may remain inaccessible to a wheelchair user. An evacuation plan may offer no practical way for a person with a visual, hearing, or intellectual disability to understand a warning, reach safety or seek assistance.
This is the gap Bangladesh must confront.
Disability inclusion is often treated as a social safeguard to be added after climate programs are designed. Instead, it should be used to test whether those programs are fit for purpose.
Resilience cannot be measured only by the number of shelters built or households reached, but by whether people with different accessibility needs can benefit.
The evidence is difficult to ignore. The United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction’s (UNDRR) 2023 Global Survey on Persons with Disabilities and Disasters , based on 6,342 responses from 132 countries, found that only 8% of respondents said local disaster-risk-reduction plans addressed the specific needs of persons with disabilities.
Only 11% reported awareness of national-level disaster-risk-reduction plans. More tellingly, 86% said they had not participated in community-level disaster planning. These findings expose a persistent gap between commitments to inclusion and the realities of disaster preparedness.
Bangladesh has its own evidence. A study by the Centre for Disability in Development (CDD) in Patharghata, Barguna, and Assasuni, Satkhira, surveyed 300 children and young people with disabilities aged 6 to 25. The findings showed that 93% believed extreme weather events had worsened over the previous five years, while 80% felt that persons with disabilities were more severely affected than other vulnerable groups.
More concerningly, 80% said they were not prioritized during evacuation, and 57% reported discrimination in accessing relief. 87% required regular healthcare, yet only 20% could access it. Riverbank erosion, salinity, cyclones, and flooding disrupted healthcare, education, mobility, and livelihoods.
Disasters affect not only people with disabilities but can also cause new disabilities. Injuries, psychological trauma, interrupted treatment, and the lack of rehabilitation or assistive devices can turn an emergency into a lifelong challenge. Inclusive climate action must therefore cover prevention, evacuation, healthcare, rehabilitation, and recovery -- not just relief.
The seven-point policy proposal, unveiled in Dhaka on November 5 by the National Platform for Disability-Inclusive Disaster Risk Reduction and Climate Change Adaptation with technical support from CDD, has brought these concerns to the fore ahead of COP31.
Its recommendations include accessible warning systems and shelters, dedicated climate finance, rehabilitation, participation in policy-making, and disability-disaggregated data. The task now is to translate these recommendations into budgets, standards, institutional responsibilities, and measurable results.
That requires changing how climate projects are planned and assessed. Every publicly funded shelter, evacuation route, warning system, and emergency health facility should be assessed for accessibility before approval and again once operational.
Accessibility also requires safe toilets, usable sleeping areas, clear signage, accessible communication, and arrangements for people who need personal assistance.
Warnings should be issued through multiple channels -- audio, visual, text, and sign-language formats -- so that no single mode of communication becomes a point of failure.
Climate finance must follow the same principle. Bangladesh is seeking substantial support from international partners to implement its climate commitments. It should also demonstrate how much of that investment addresses the barriers faced by persons with disabilities.
Accessibility costs should be built into project budgets from the outset, rather than treated as optional add-ons when funds remain. Dedicated allocations matter, but so does ensuring that mainstream adaptation projects are inclusive by design.
Participation is equally important. Organizations of persons with disabilities should have meaningful roles on local disaster management committees and in the design, monitoring, and evaluation of climate programs.
Consultation after a project has been designed is not meaningful participation, and counting beneficiaries does not prove that people have influenced decisions. Their experiences should help determine what is built, where it is located, and how its effectiveness is measured.
Women and girls with disabilities can face additional barriers to safe evacuation, sanitation, healthcare, protection, and livelihoods. Programs that consider gender and disability separately may fail to reach those facing both forms of exclusion. Their specific needs must inform climate adaptation, not be treated as an afterthought.
For Bangladesh, COP31 offers an opportunity to link disability inclusion with broader negotiations on adaptation, climate finance, and loss and damage. However, international advocacy will carry greater weight if matched by domestic implementation.
The National Adaptation Plan 2023–2050 and the Standing Orders on Disaster 2019 provide frameworks to strengthen inclusion. The next step is to assign clear institutional responsibilities, allocate resources, and publish measurable indicators of progress.
When warnings are inaccessible, evacuation becomes more difficult and dangerous. Shelters that exclude certain users fail to protect the whole community, while gaps in rehabilitation can leave families with prolonged care responsibilities and lost income. Designing for accessibility from the outset helps public investment deliver its intended benefits.
Bangladesh has made considerable progress in cyclone preparedness and community-based disaster management. The next measure of that progress should be whether people with disabilities can participate in and benefit from the systems built to protect them. Resilience means that every member of a community can prepare, reach safety, recover and rebuild with dignity.
At COP31, Bangladesh should argue that accessibility should be at the centre of climate justice. At home, it should demonstrate what that commitment means in practice. A climate-resilient country cannot be built around an imagined average citizen. It must work for everyone.

item.title: The land we share: Bangladesh’s stories of harmony
item.description:
In a village in Indian Punjab, 87-year-old Gajju Khan is waiting for a sound he has not heard for most of his life. He wants to live long enough to hear the call to prayer from the mosque now being built in Jakhiwal.
What makes the story more striking is who is building it. Local Sikhs and Hindus have given money, bricks, cement, and land so that their Muslim neighbours can finally have a place to pray.
Independent journalist Cheena Kapoor wrote about this in a photo essay published on October 28, 2026 . It shows villagers restoring mosques that were abandoned after the violence and mass displacement of the 1947 Partition.
One of them is Bibi Rajinder Kaur, a Sikh woman who persuaded her grandson to donate the family’s farmland for the mosque. Her reasoning was simple. The other community has a place to gather. The local Muslims do not.
The Partition tore countless families apart, and the wound has been carried from one generation to the next. That is why the weight of this effort is so great. There are no grand declarations about tolerance here. It began with a piece of land, an unmet need, and a few neighbours willing to stand by.
As the mosque rises, something invisible is being joined to it: The everyday trust of living side by side.
Bangladesh has its own stories too, and they are not cast in one mould. In some places there are mutual gifts of land, in others a closed place of worship has been allowed to reopen, and in others neighbours have quietly made sure no one in the community went without what they needed.
A mosque and a crematorium in Bagerhat
In Fakirhat, Bagerhat, two people of different faiths each met a need of the other’s community. According to a report published in April 2022 , Pranab Kumar Ghosh, a Hindu college teacher, donated land for a mosque, while Sheikh Mizanur Rahman, a local Muslim politician, gave land for a Hindu crematorium.
After the Dhaka-Khulna highway opened, Attaki Mor (crossing) became much busier. Shopkeepers and passers-by there struggled to find a place to pray. On the land Ghosh gave, a small prayer room was built first, and a larger mosque grew up around it later.
The crematorium problem was of a different kind. The old one on the bank of the Bhairab river had been swallowed by the river, leaving Hindu families with nowhere to perform last rites. Mizanur Rahman, who owned the adjoining land, gave a portion of it for a new crematorium.
The needs were different, but the understanding was the same: You respect your neighbour’s religious obligations even when they are not your own.
Ghosh’s college later recognized his contribution, and local leaders held up both initiatives as examples of harmony. Most striking of all, the generosity went both ways, and neither man was asked to embrace the other’s faith.
A temple reopens after 47 years in Rajshahi
In Rajshahi, generosity took the form of an unlocked door. Regular puja had not been held at the Khojapur Sarbojanin Shib and Kali Matar Mondir (temple) since 1975. The land the temple stands on had been bought by Korban Ali, a Muslim businessman.
When local devotees wanted to reopen the temple, he agreed. In March 2022, devotees returned to observe Maha Shivratri, and to make the way easier, Ali even removed two mango trees himself.
A report captures the emotion and weight of that first major puja in 47 years. The path to the temple had become hard to reach, and Ali let the devotees walk through his own land.
No land changed hands here, yet the episode matters just as much. Ownership of land could easily have meant a locked gate. Ali instead made room for his Hindu neighbours.
A reopened temple cannot erase decades of silence, but it has given one community back a place tied to its faith and history.
When the state makes room
Government institutions have given land too. In October 2018, the then prime minister announced a gift of about one and a half bigha of adjoining land to the Dhakeshwari Temple, one of the country’s most important Hindu places of worship.
In August 2025, Bangladesh Railway allotted land in Dhaka’s Joar Sahara area for two mosques and a Hindu temple at a nominal price set by the railway authority.
These were not acts of personal kindness, and it would be wrong to read them that way. One was the announcement of a political leader holding public office, the other an institutional allocation.
Their value lies in a public message: Different communities in the same city need safe places to worship. But how much of that value becomes real depends on what happens after the announcement: The legal transfer, how the land is used, and whether the institution can actually put it to use.
Where land is held by a public agency, transparent rules and fair access matter most.
Interfaith help is not always about land. A two-day Harinam Moha yogga of Matua devotees, held in April 2026, took place at Bangladesh Ashwini Sebashram in Ganga Channa village, Chitalmari upazila, Bagerhat. There were rituals, devotional songs, and a local fair. People of other faiths, including Muslims, volunteered to provide water, resting arrangements, and other services.
These acts may seem modest, but big gatherings run on help passed from hand to hand. A neighbour who offers water or shelter can be part of the event without taking part in the rituals. The only thing asked in return is that we give a neighbour’s festival the same consideration we hope for our own.
A neighbour’s land, a young man’s future
Generosity can reach beyond places of worship. According to a report published in October 2026, a Hindu resident of Juri in Moulvibazar donated some land to his Muslim neighbour. The young man had got a job at Sonali Bank but ran into trouble during the recruitment verification. His family lived in a rented house, and no immovable property was registered in his father’s name. The land was given free of charge, and the donor also paid the registration costs. A sub-registrar confirmed the transfer, though the report did not name the parties.
This was not a gift for a mosque, temple or church, yet it belongs to the same story: How people respond to one another’s needs across religious lines.
Sometimes the most meaningful help is not a building or a public event. It is an opportunity that might otherwise have been lost.
Religious communities have also stood together by donating land for their own places of worship. In Chittagong, former president Ziaur Rahman gave land for the Purnachar International Buddhist Temple and guest house, as mentioned in a report.
Three acres of land donated by a parish secretary and other members in Tangail helped establish St John’s Church in Sridampara village, where about 65 Garo families worship. Neither account proves donations across faiths, but both show how land and community contributions can sustain religious life.
Harmony does not mean the absence of disagreement
These stories are not all of one kind. Some are personal generosity, some are government decisions, some are practical help, and each has to be understood in its own context. Nor does a handful of good examples mean that religious minorities never face discrimination, insecurity, or property disputes.
Harmony cannot be measured by counting how many temples, mosques, and churches stand side by side. It depends on whether people can worship freely, whether property rights are protected, whether the authorities settle disputes fairly, and whether neighbours can trust one another without fear.
A donation can be generous, but the chance to worship should never depend on one landowner’s goodwill. It is a right, and state institutions must protect it.
The Rajshahi temple stayed shut for 47 years and reopened only because one owner agreed, which is exactly the kind of fragility a right is meant to remove. Empathy strengthens the bonds of coexistence, but it cannot replace equal citizenship, accountability, and the rule of law.
That is why these stories should be told without exaggeration. They do not prove that harmony has been won for good. They only show that people can make it possible in their own neighbourhoods if they choose to.
In Punjab, an old man waits for the call to prayer. In Bagerhat, land gave one community a place to pray and another a place for last rites. In Rajshahi, a temple door opened after decades. In Dhaka, public land has been set aside for different faiths. In Moulvibazar, a neighbour’s small plot secured a young man’s future.
The circumstances differ from place to place. The principle stays the same: Nothing says that another person’s faith, grief, festival, or need has to set us apart.
A piece of land cannot erase the violence of history, and one generous act cannot guarantee a peaceful future. But when people make room for one another, they build something no declaration can: A place where neighbours can pray, mourn, celebrate and belong.
Perhaps that is where harmony begins, with the recognition that everyone has a right to dignity, safety and a place in society, and that protecting it is a public duty, not a private favour.
Nafew Sajed Joy is a Bangladeshi researcher, writer and environmental activist. He has a deep interest in sustainable development, development issues and South Asian affairs.

item.title: General strike over housing hits Spain ahead of election
item.description:
Protesters disrupted the morning commute for hundreds of thousands of Spaniards on Wednesday as a general strike centred on the country’s chronic housing crisis began weeks before a snap election.
Unions reported a “massive” early uptake in Spain’s first nationwide 24-hour stoppage since 2012, which also aims to raise pressure on wages and public services, but business leaders played down the participation.
The size of demonstrations planned in Madrid and Barcelona will be seen as an indicator of public discontent before the November 29 vote, which the right-wing opposition is predicted to win.
The impact on industry and services in the European Union’s fourth-largest economy will also be scrutinized, as pickets were organized at logistics centers, industrial estates and on motorways across the country.
In Madrid, dozens of protesters braved the rain and blocked a main road leading into the center of the Spanish capital, causing tailbacks, but many shops opened as normal.
Public transport suffered disruption even with the implementation of minimum service requirements for commuter trains, metros and buses.
In Barcelona, the metro and bus networks were out of action until the late afternoon after offering minimum services during the morning rush hour.
In contrast, Madrid’s metro reported that 93 percent of its trains ran in the early morning, although passenger numbers were down by around half.
UGT union leader Pepe Alvarez told public broadcaster RTVE that the participation was “massive,” with a “total” stoppage in some regions making the strike “a huge success.”
But UGT spokesman Rafael Espartero acknowledged participation was “uneven,” with large mobilization in the car manufacturing, petrochemicals and meat sectors and in coastal regions, where he said housing difficulties were acute.
The CEOE organization, which represents business leaders, said in a statement that the impact varied by region and area of work, with a “low participation” in most sectors.
The main UGT and CCOO unions called the strike following a wave of nationwide protests over access to housing, sparked by the eviction in September of an 87-year-old Madrid pensioner.
The demonstrations included a five-week occupation of Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square, where hundreds of tents were pitched, sparking imitations in other cities.
Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called the election, initially scheduled for 2027, after his minority government failed to secure parliamentary approval for a package of housing measures proposed in response to the protests.
Sanchez, who has governed since 2018 but trails in most polls, has urged voters to defend hard-won rights including public healthcare, the eight-hour working day and pensions amid warnings from his Socialists that the right could roll them back.
But the unions have insisted the strike is directed against all levels of the state and not only the right, which voted down the government’s housing decrees.
The Socialists and the main right-wing opposition Popular Party (PP) “must listen to us, because the streets are speaking clearly”, UGT leader Alvarez said on Wednesday.
Business groups and the right have rejected the strike, seeing an election-related gambit instead of a genuine labor dispute.
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo, who leads most polls, warned that unions risked being linked to Sanchez “forever” if they went ahead with the strike.
Feijoo has also called it a “serious mistake” following a high-speed train collision last month in central Spain that killed 69 people.
Union leaders have defended the walkout as an exceptional measure intended to generate broad social pressure for action on soaring housing costs.
They are demanding a larger public housing stock, a ban on evicting vulnerable tenants as well as rent controls and restrictions on tourist accommodation in areas suffering the greatest stress.

item.title: US Republicans derail bid to impeach Pentagon chief
item.description:
Republicans in the US House of Representatives on Tuesday blocked an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war, handing President Donald Trump a victory days after his party’s crushing midterm election defeat.
The House voted 211 to 204 to send the impeachment resolution to the Judiciary Committee, effectively derailing a planned vote Wednesday on whether to bring formal charges against the embattled Pentagon chief.
The resolution was introduced by Republican Thomas Massie, a Trump critic who was the only member of his party to oppose the procedural maneuver, according to US media.
The impeachment drive had threatened to deepen Trump’s troubles after Democrats swept last week’s midterms, with anger at the sputtering Iran war and soaring fuel prices helping drive voters to a historic rejection of Republicans.
Republicans still hold a narrow House majority until January, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. And 11 Democrats missed the vote.
Trump hailed the procedural defeat as an “EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot,” in a post on Truth Social, while Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell, in a post on X, called the vote as a “TOTAL VICTORY!”
“We look forward to ending this sham impeachment in the committee room, where facts will continue to prevail and this distraction can be put to rest,” Parnell added.
Hegseth earlier Tuesday dismissed the impeachment effort as a “farce” and defended his record leading the Iran war and other military operations under Trump.
“It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it,” he said at a Pentagon press conference, branding the accusations “slander” and “sabotage.”
Moments after Hegseth’s televised appearance, Trump signaled his support.
“Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS,” the 80-year-old president wrote on his Truth Social platform.
Vice President JD Vance also backed the defense secretary, saying he had “obviously not” committed impeachable offenses.
Massie’s eight articles of impeachment accused Hegseth of illegally waging war without congressional authorization and abusing his powers as Pentagon chief.
Several related to the eight-month Iran war, accusing him of violating the War Powers Resolution, which places limits on US military interventions without congressional authorization.
Other allegations involved the 2025 conflict with Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which Massie branded “extrajudicial killings.”
He also accused Hegseth of suppressing free speech by trying to punish Democratic Senator Mark Kelly over a video urging military and intelligence personnel to refuse illegal orders.
Hegseth defended the operations in Yemen, Iran, Venezuela and against alleged drug smugglers, while seeking to equate the impeachment effort with an attack on US troops.
“I stand behind every one of these operations. I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow,” he said.
The decision to send the resolution to committee halts the immediate impeachment drive but does not prevent Democrats from reviving the effort after taking control of Congress in January.
Massie, who lost his Republican primary to a Trump-backed challenger, will leave Congress at the end of his term.

item.title: World leaders take stage at COP31 but big names missing
item.description:
World leaders will take the stage at COP31 in Turkiye on Wednesday but some prominent names are missing from this year’s annual UN climate summit even as global warming intensifies.
The two-week conference kicked off earlier this week in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya, with governments under pressure to tackle the climate crisis after a year of heatwaves in Europe, deadly floods in Nepal and major wildfires in Indonesia.
Dozens of leaders will speak during the “high-level segment” taking place on Wednesday and Thursday, including Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Iran’s Masoud Pezeshkian.
But observers have pointed to the absence of some big names, with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham the only leader from a G7 country scheduled to address the summit.
While European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen is coming to Antalya, French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni are skipping the event.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi are also absent from the most recent list.
“It is a shame that some of the bigger European leaders aren’t coming. We need Europe to be showing up strongly at this COP,” Cosima Cassel, a climate diplomacy expert at think-tank E3G, told AFP.
Wopke Hoekstra, the EU’s top climate official, said the absences were “not completely atypical” as leaders may have “practical” reasons for not being able to attend a summit.
But he also told reporters in Brussels that “expectations are not necessarily high” for this climate conference.
Iran’s Pezeshkian said he would use the event as an opportunity to express Tehran’s position on environmental destruction in war.
“At this conference, we will speak about the actions of the United States and Israel in destroying the environment,” he said before departing for Turkiye, according to Iranian state television.
The French government said Macron would be absent because November 11 is World War I Armistice Day and the president will attend an EU summit in Ireland on Thursday.
“If top leaders want influence over where the global (energy) transition is going, showing up is a pretty good place to start,” said Chiara Martinelli, director of Climate Action Network Europe.
“I am afraid that Ursula von der Leyen will be lonely on the stage while the leaders of the biggest EU economies are a no-show,” Martinelli said.
Unsurprisingly, US President Donald Trump, who pulled the United States out of the Paris Agreement and has not sent officials to climate talks since his re-election in 2024, is not attending the summit.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, who rarely attends COPs, will be represented by Vice President Han Zheng.
The United States and China are the world’s top economies and biggest emitters of planet-heating emissions, making their presence at climate talks crucial to the process.
“But we have Lula,” Cassel said.
Climate campaigners breathed a huge sigh of relief when Lula, who has championed cutting deforestation rates, defeated right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro in last month’s Brazilian presidential election.
COP31 host Turkiye is championing a voluntary initiative to accelerate the electrification of transport, buildings and industry, with a target of raising electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35% by 2035.
The EU has stressed that electrification must be “clean,” which could spark debate over the role of oil, gas and coal in the Turkish proposal.
Since agreeing in 2023 for the first time to transition away from fossil fuels -- the main driver of climate change -- nations have struggled to advance that goal at the annual COP conferences.

item.title: US judge rejects BBC bid to dismiss Trump defamation suit
item.description:
A federal judge has allowed US President Donald Trump’s multibillion-dollar defamation suit against the BBC to proceed, rejecting a bid by the British broadcaster to dismiss the case.
Trump has accused the BBC of deceptively editing a documentary to make it seem as if he was inciting violence when he told supporters to march on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021.
He has sought at least $5 billion each for one claim of defamation and a separate claim under a Florida consumer protection law.
US District Judge Jeffrey T Kuntz on Tuesday rejected the BBC’s bid to dismiss the defamation suit, but tossed the Florida protection law claim.
A spokesperson for the BBC said in a brief statement that the broadcaster was “surprised by this decision” but respected the court’s authority.
“We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process,” the statement added.
Trump, in a Truth Social post, hailed the judge’s ruling as “A Huge Victory.”
“We will continue fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People!” he added.
The BBC documentary at issue spliced together two separate sections of Trump’s speech on January 6, 2021, making it appear that he had explicitly urged supporters to attack the US Capitol.
While the broadcaster has apologized for the incident, which prompted the resignation of multiple senior executives, it has denied causing Trump any real injury.
In a 40-page ruling, Kuntz wrote: “Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day.”
He added: “Given the time disparity between the two statements, the distance itself tends toward a plausible inference that BBC knew or should have known that the segment they were creating would not and could not have been a truthful statement.
“This was not trimming around the edges but creating something different than what was stated in the speech.”
Last month, Trump faced a setback in the case when a magistrate judge ordered him to give a deposition by December 11, after the BBC claimed he was dodging their efforts to get sworn testimony.
Trump risks sanctions if he fails to attend the deposition by then, including the potential dismissal of his lawsuit, the court said.

item.title: Police seal Sylhet resort where fugitive ex-MP Ranjit held meeting
item.description:
Police have sealed Sohel Square Eco Resort in Ratargul, Gowainghat, Sylhet, after fugitive former Sunamganj-1 MP Ranjit Sarkar held a meeting there, triggering widespread controversy.
According to Gowainghat police, the resort was sealed on Wednesday.
Repeated calls to Gowainghat police station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Md Omar Faruk went unanswered. However, duty officer Sub-Inspector Hasib said the Sohel Square Resort in Ratargul was shut down by police around 3am.
Four people, including two resort employees and two Awami League leaders and activists, have been detained in connection with the incident. Police said preparations for filing a case were underway.
According to police and other sources, a lawyer rented the resort on November 8, claiming he would organise an educational tour. More than 150 people arrived at the venue by bus around 3pm and took part in various activities.
Ranjit, joint secretary of Sylhet district Awami League, later appeared at the resort, put up a separate banner, delivered a brief speech and left shortly afterwards.
In a video circulated on social media, he was heard saying that he had held a rally with party leaders and activists after entering the country. He also vowed to continue the struggle until Sheikh Hasina returned to Bangladesh and urged activists to prepare for a final fight.
Ranjit had been in hiding since August 5, 2024, and was reportedly staying in the United Kingdom for a period.
He uploaded the meeting's video to his Facebook account at 4:49pm on Monday. Hours after the footage went viral, an agitated group set fire to his house in Gopaltilla, Sylhet city.
Sunamganj police later arrested Tahirpur upazila Awami League Organising Secretary Tara Mia after identifying him in the video. He was subsequently sent to jail on a court order.
Sources said the meeting was organised under the leadership of local Awami League and Jubo League leaders, including Farid Ahmed Shamim, Aminur Rahman Chowdhury and Masuk Ahmed.
Meanwhile, Ranjit's whereabouts remain unknown. In a WhatsApp conversation with a news outlet, he claimed the meeting was held inside Bangladesh, in his electoral constituency, with only local residents attending.
Acknowledging that the Awami League was banned, he said party leaders would hold programmes wherever they found an opportunity.

item.title: Hasnat questions fertilizer dealership appointments over alleged nepotism
item.description:
Questions over alleged favoritism in the distribution of fertilizer dealerships have emerged after claims that relatives of sitting lawmakers were among those awarded dealerships under a nationwide appointment process.
Hasnat Abdullah, member of parliament for Comilla-4, alleged that the beneficiaries included the wives, sons, nieces and other relatives of sitting MPs, raising concerns over transparency in the selection process.
He said the appointment process was marked by unprecedented corruption and asked the agriculture minister whether it would be reconsidered.
The opposition MP raised the allegations in a supplementary question to the minister during Wednesday afternoon's parliamentary session, presided over by Deputy Speaker Barrister Kaiser Kamal.
Citing several newspaper headlines, Hasnat told the House: “An MP's son, brother-in-law and nephew's wife have become fertilizer dealers. In Thakurgaon, 28 of the 31 dealers are affiliated with the BNP, and 10 of them are wives, children and nieces of party leaders.”
He also noted that a Chhatra Dal leader had been fatally attacked in Natore and that a child of an MP was also alleged to have received a dealership.
Hasnat described the appointments as a “grand festival” of favoritism.
Addressing the minister, he asked whether the irregularities were premeditated, whether the appointments would be reviewed, and when MPs would cease to exploit their positions for the commercial benefit of themselves and their families.
Agriculture Minister Mohammad Amin Ur Rashid responded that 2 committees had been constituted to oversee the appointments: one at the upazila level, chaired by the Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO), and another at the district level, chaired by the Deputy Commissioner (DC).
He said applications had been invited under specified rules and conditions, and that the ministry had instructed both committees to adhere strictly to those rules.
According to the minister, applications were first forwarded to the upazila level, where the UNO-led committee, together with the upazila agriculture officer, the relevant local agriculture officer and local dignitaries, conducted the initial scrutiny.
The vetted proposals were then submitted to the DC's office, where the district committee reviewed them and sent a ranked list of 3 candidates to the ministry.
The ministry declared the first-ranked candidate the dealer.
The minister added that the district committee comprised the district agriculture officer, the DC and other relevant officials. All proposals reached the ministry bearing the signatures of every committee member rather than that of any single individual.
